doc.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Sleazy bars, Willie the Lion Smith and Jimmy Ryan's
summary: Ingham loves smoky bars and recalls working at Jimmy Ryan's with Max Kaminsky and Roy Eldridge before the block was demolished.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah, because also the music had a sense of fun to it. And I like those clubs where people were drinking and talking and romancing and flirting and were quarreling and fighting, and the music’s going on and everything is all, it’s all part of life. And I think that’s why the jazz sounded that way, it had so much color and flare and fervor and if you like, drunken whatever. I love those places, those sleazy bars. It’s wonderful. You get just a piano player. People would tell me Willie “The Lion” Smith would be playing in a joint, and there’d be just a few drunks and as somebody says, a couple of ladies at the bar who use more lipstick than deodorant. And Willie’d be playing there and apparently, just to keep atmosphere in the joint, he’d just be vamping [scats] and just looking around. You know, there’s hardly anybody in there, but he’d be playing that, just to get something going. And then people would fall in. I think I just got in the tail end of that when I worked in Jimmy Ryan’s in New York, and that was that sort of place, you know, you could smell the toilet from the entrance. You know you’re up on the bandstand, and they watered down the drinks, and everything. But it was part of the old thing. And I worked there with Max Kaminsky, who was one of my favorite trumpet players, and Roy Eldridge was there during the week, and Max did the weekends. And it was just pretty much the end of that when I got here, ‘80, ‘81, ‘82. And then that whole street, it had another version of Condon’s club next to Ryan’s, on 54th Street, and then I think the Prudential Insurance Company decided, they bought the whole block and demolished it to make a car park so that went. So corporate America struck again.
Well I’m glad that there seems to be at least a small and loyal market for the kind of music that you’re fond of. © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
